summary:
Mars Route Planner (MRP) is a web app for planning a Marswalk (EVA) in Jezero crater. The astronaut marks a start point and science stops on a map built from several NASA missions (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA). The app computes a safe route over the real relief, avoiding slopes of 25° and more, and estimates the time and oxygen with a walking model scaled to Mars gravity. The EVA can be replayed in 2D or 3D.

The challenge asks for an integrated, layered view of one Martian site that answers three questions. MRP shows where to go and at what cost, comparing the return to the habitat and to the start. It shows current conditions from the latest Perseverance MEDA data. It also highlights which science targets are worth visiting and which mission revealed each one.

On Mars, a bad route can mean running out of oxygen. MRP gives a GO / NO-GO verdict with a 10% O₂ reserve and marks the point of no return. Every layer cites its mission and date, and every estimate is labeled as one, so planners can trust what they see.
details:
Mars Route Planner (MRP) is a web app for planning a Marswalk in Jezero crater. The astronaut marks a start point and science stops on a map built from NASA mission data (MRO HiRISE and CTX, Mars Odyssey THEMIS, MGS MOLA). An A* algorithm then finds a safe route over the real terrain, avoiding slopes of 25° and more. A walking model scaled to Mars gravity estimates the time and oxygen of each plan. With the 0.73 kg of oxygen of NASA’s lunar suit design and a 10% reserve, the app gives a GO / NO-GO verdict for returning to the habitat or to the start. It also marks the point of no return and can reorder the stops to save oxygen. The EVA can be replayed in 2D or 3D, and a Conditions screen shows the latest Perseverance MEDA weather data.

Its main benefit is making the most critical limit visible before going outside: will the oxygen last? Every layer cites its mission and date, and every estimate is labeled as one, so planners know what is measured and what is modeled.

We built it with TypeScript, React, Leaflet and CesiumJS, and processed the NASA data with Python. It is a static site on Cloudflare, so it runs on any browser, including phones. Its creative core is turning a route into a survival decision, while staying transparent about every assumption.

This project is an MVP, ready to expand by processing more data. The Python pipeline turns NASA rasters into light files with a fixed format, and the routing engine works on any grid in that format. Adding new landing sites, finer terrain, more map layers or a longer MEDA weather history means running the pipeline on new data, not rewriting the app.
